The hostel common room was loud with balloons and cake. Tushar noticed Nikita standing by the window, a paper plate untouched in her hand.
“You okay?” Tushar asked quietly.
“Just tired.”
“Okay. I'm not going to make you smile. But you don't have to hold that plate like a shield.” Nikita laughed a little in spite of herself.
“Sorry, it's a good party.”
“It is. And it's fine if you're somewhere else in your head tonight.” Tushar took a piece of cake and stood by the window. “I'm just going to stand here and eat this badly.”
After a while Nikita said, “My grandfather's anniversary is tomorrow.”
“Thanks for telling me,” Tushar said. “Want to walk to the canteen after?”

qa.a: Nikita held a paper plate, untouched.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nikita when Tushar says it is fine to be somewhere else in her head?
qa.a: It may bring relief, since Nikita no longer has to act cheerful, and it made room to mention the anniversary.

passage: I'm Preeti, and at a wedding last spring I noticed Samir, a friend from college, at the far end of the table. Everyone else was dancing to the band, and Samir sat with a plate of rice, watching the floor. A cousin pulled at Samir's arm, “Come, come,” and Samir shook a head with a polite smile. I nearly did the same, dragged Samir to the dance floor and told a joke. Instead I sat down and asked, “Do you want company or space?” After a pause Samir said, “Company. Just not talking.” We watched the dancers for ten minutes without a word. Later Samir told me the old office had let go of most of the team. I hadn't known.

qa.q: What did Samir have on the plate while sitting at the far end of the table?
qa.a: Samir had a plate of rice.

qa.q: Why did Preeti ask, “Do you want company or space?”
qa.a: Preeti felt concerned for Samir and wanted to care without pushing, letting Samir choose how much closeness to have.

qa.q: What could Preeti do in the weeks after the wedding?
qa.a: Preeti could check in with Samir now and then, ask how the job hunt is going, and offer help without pressing.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling while the others danced?
qa.a: Samir was probably worried and low about losing the job, and did not feel like joining the celebration, which fits the plate of rice and the polite smile.

I have given him leave for the weekend and asked Chetan to keep an eye out.

passage:
Journal, Saturday night.
Chechi's wedding reception was loud and wonderful. The band played, everyone danced, Appa even sang. But I kept noticing Varun. He came, he smiled for the photos, and then he sat by the fairy lights near the gate, turning his phone over and over.
Around ten, I took two bowls of payasam and sat next to him. I didn't ask him to dance. I just said, 'You've been quiet. No pressure, but I'm here.' He said his parents are separating and he didn't want to spoil the day. I told him he wasn't spoiling anything. We ate the payasam and watched the dancing for a while. He left early, but at midnight he texted: 'Thanks for not making me dance.'
Jomon

qa.q: Where was Varun sitting?
qa.a: By the fairy lights near the gate.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling while watching Varun?
qa.a: Jomon felt concerned, noticing Varun smiling only for photos and turning the phone over and over.

qa.q: What did Jomon's check-in get right?
qa.a: It was gentle and pressure-free ('No pressure, but I'm here'), didn't push Varun to dance, and let him leave when he needed to.

qa.q: How did Varun feel about joining the celebration?
qa.a: He was sad about his parents separating and worried about spoiling the day, and felt grateful not to be made to dance.

passage: At the Holi gathering in the lane behind the Pandharpur temple, everyone was pink and shrieking. Irawati, colour in her hair, noticed Kishore on the steps of the grain shop, shirt still clean, turning a steel glass of thandai in his hands. Last year he had been the first to throw colour. His cousins waved at him; he waved back and didn't move. Someone yelled, "Kishore, come on, don't be boring!" Irawati wiped her hands on her dupatta and sat on the step beside him, not too close. "Too much noise today?" she asked. He shrugged. "Baba's not well. Didn't feel like it." "Okay," she said. "I'll sit here a bit." She didn't dab colour on him. After a while, he tipped a little green onto her palm himself.

qa.q: What was Kishore holding on the steps?
qa.a: He was turning a steel glass of thandai in his hands.

qa.q: What was Irawati thinking when she noticed Kishore's clean shirt?
qa.a: She was concerned, because he had been the first to throw colour last year, and she sensed something was wrong.

qa.q: Why did Irawati's way of checking in work?
qa.a: She asked one gentle question, accepted his answer, and sat with him without pushing colour or cheer on him, so he could join in at his own pace.

qa.q: What might the shout of "don't be boring" have felt like for Kishore?
qa.a: It probably felt heavy and lonely, as if his worry about Baba had to be hidden to please the crowd.
